As digital business operations continue to expand at a fast pace, it has become imperative for all companies to reconsider their strategies for addressing customer inquiries and concerns. In the case of technology firms, the number of questions received each day is often substantial and ranges from general service-related queries to more technical questions regarding compatibility, among others. Human-based customer service channels create operational challenges, inconsistencies, and delays, particularly after regular working hours.
In this paper, we outline the design and implementation of a chatbot system powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that has been
to address customer service-related inquiries for

Solutions, a software development and consulting firm operating out of Noida, Uttar Pradesh. The system is primarily geared towards handling customer inquiries within the following four key service areas: application development, website design, IT consulting, and legal technology services. Using the

feature of Google Cloud's natural language processing capability, the chatbot can receive inputs from users in various forms and determine their intent and entities without imposing strict conditions on input types.

From an architectural point of view three layer can be distinguished. First layer is front-end (web-based chatting interface created by HTML, CSS and JavaScript technologies). Next layer is Node.js application (using Express.js framework) that is responsible for routing messages, managing chat session, and writing ticket information to the cloud hosted MongoDB Atlas database. Third layer is Python based Flask application (administrator panel that provides possibility to observe and manage the all-active chats in real-time, change ticket status, add private notes, and send manual answer to the user through chat). Now in administrator panel is implemented a 'Human Handoff' section where synchronization between agent and customer chat is available in real-time enabling manual chat intervention by agent.

The main factor in the described architecture is to choose a distributed MongoDB database as the sync between the Node.js application and the Flask application. This made possible to avoid the need for an extra database and servers. At the same time the data generated by the one application was available for the other. The live sync with poll method took approximately ten seconds after generation of the new data on the dashboard side.
The whole system has been developed, tested, and documented in this project cycle. Tests have included

intent accuracy, message handling from beginning to end, workflow for creating tickets and updating their status, platform-specific encoding consistency, and synchronization between two apps in real time. All the expected test cases were passed successfully, and the problems identified throughout the development process, which include
entity format validation failure, an encoding issue for Windows, and cross-application path resolving, were recorded and fixed.

These findings prove that a well-engineered chatbot system can significantly lighten the load on the customer service staff and yet ensure an acceptable level of answer quality appreciated by the end-users. It automatically processes regular questions, passes complicated ones to human representatives along with all the context, and allows the admin team to control everything from one panel. This document presents the full cycle of creating a chatbot, from requirement analysis to deployment and beyond.

Solutions, there is a larger role for this project to play. Each of the architectural decisions, design patterns and implementation steps outlined within this document can be applied to any SME IT company looking to introduce a conversational AI layer on top of their website. This layered approach with the chatbot back-end, admin panel, and NLP component clearly separated will make upgrading and potentially replacing any one of these elements over time in accordance with business needs far simpler. This document should be considered both an account of what was implemented, and as a guide for anyone wishing to implement a similar service in the future

As a company tries to assess potential software developers, there is no time for the nine-to-five routine. A CEO who works till late evening to prepare for an important board meeting needs to know if the developer is capable of creating a cross-platform application based on .NET MAUI framework. What was clearly required was an intelligent system capable of engaging in dialogues, adjusting to individual phrasings, and transferring calls to live agents where appropriate.

The 27 intent design tries to find a trade-off between inclusiveness and feasibility. A service with too few intents cannot capture the nuances between semantically different user intentions and thus responds to queries generically where specificity would have been preferred. A system with too many intents is prone to being overly specific, causing slight wording changes to fire wrong intents given the small amount of training phrases available for each intent. The 27 intent system was obtained by means of experimentation: candidates for the intent set were tested for classification accuracy, and pairs of intents that always confused one another were either merged or augmented with new training phrases.

chatbot utilizes a sophisticated decision tree logic to handle user queries. By categorizing inputs into four primary
domains—Informational, Plans, Operational, and Administrative—the system ensures that users receive targeted automated responses while seamlessly escalating complex technical
issues or billing inquiries to the human handoff and ticketing modules via MongoDB integration.

The process of intent classification proceeds through a defined decision tree. The system first determines the available context, by checking the active contexts from the current session, which helps bias the classification towards relevant intents. It then compares the user utterance against each of the defined intents, to determine the confidence that it matches each intent. If the highest confidence exceeds the set threshold of 0.30, that intent will be activated and its fulfillment text returned. If no intent meets the threshold, the Default
Fallback Intent will be activated and will inform the user they should make use of the quick actions and contact the support team.
Entity extraction happens in conjunction with intent classification. After an intent has been identified,

will parse the user utterance for any matches for the configured entity types - service-type, platform-type, tech-stack, and project-phase - and extract the value of the match. The entity values will be available in the fulfillment text, and in systems that use webhooks, to backend code to provide for customized responses. Entities are being used in this implementation for context, and for annotation, but not for dynamically forming responses.

The automatic priority assignment logic represents an early triage mechanism that reduces the cognitive load on the admin team. Without automated triage, every incoming ticket requires human judgement to determine its urgency before any action can be taken. By pre-assigning priority based on service area — where legal technology queries are designated High priority due to the time-sensitive nature of trial preparation work — the system allows the admin team to sort the ticket queue by priority and attend to the most urgent tickets first without reading through each one individually.

module could not access the file. This happened due to the relative path construction, which uses the current module's path to find the intended target.
-flask is actually located at one level up in the repository tree. Therefore, data saved in the Node.js module was not accessible in the Flask dashboard, and vice versa. The

module was adjusted with a graceful failure: if it is unable to verify the intended path at run time, it will default to a local data directory and output a clear warning to the console. Both applications will not fail silently, and the single application test can still pass without
-flask being available. Similarly, the documentation in SYNC_SETUP.md was changed and the exact folder structure was stated.
Challenge 5: Saving Session History and Completing Ticket Messages

In the process of end-to-end testing on the ticket creation workflow, it was found that newly created support ticket messages field was only containing the message that prompted the ticket creation and not the whole conversation history up to that point of time in a session. This

to the issue where the support agents looking at the ticket in the admin panel were viewing an incomplete picture of the user request, since the prior conversation was missing. The issue was located in the server.js as the function '

' was being passed only the message object at hand, and was not referring to the accumulated history for the session. To solve this, a session history is maintained on the server-side as a JavaScript object which has the session key as the key and an array of messages as its value. When a message comes in it is added to the session history array that belongs to the session regardless of it triggering the creation of a ticket. The function to create a ticket is then passed this entire session history array to create the ticket and this array is then assigned to the messages field of the ticket record.
Summary of challenges and lessons learned

In sum, the five challenges identified and detailed above yielded valuable technical lessons, both improving the system's stability and its development practice. The lessons from challenge 1 reminded the team the importance of
referring to platform documentation before undertaking operations in bulk. Challenge 2 unveiled an unexpected difference in the
entity type modeling for KINDLIST and KINDMAP which was under-represented in the platform

guides, ultimately leading to a codified convention for writing entities which was applied uniformly throughout the rest of the project. Challenge 3 served as an object lesson on the perils of system-wide defaults that differ across operating systems; it established a standard that all I/O parameters are always
defined. Challenge 4 made apparent that paths must be resolved cautiously in the context of multi-process systems, involving testing and defining the explicit

behavior for path resolution. Challenge 5 made clear that the capture of all data must be considered a testable functional requirement instead of an inherent system behavior. The resolution of these five issues produced a more resilient and portable implementation.
